title: Teresa of Ávila
hookLine: a nun who laughed, founded convents on the road, and said prayer is friendship

cards: Spain, the 1570s. A covered wagon lurches along a muddy road in the rain, pulled by mules, packed with a few nuns, their bags, and a woman nearing sixty who is running the whole operation.

Her name is Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila. She's buying houses, dealing with lawyers and bishops, borrowing money, finding cooks, and opening one small convent after another across the country.
She's funny; her letters are full of gossip, jokes and health complaints. And in the middle of all this driving and deal-making, she's well-known for prayer. Not solemn, faraway prayer.
The kind you'd have with a friend over a kitchen table.

teach.b: Teresa was born in 1515 and entered a Carmelite convent at about twenty. For almost twenty years, she says, prayer was a struggle. She was often ill, distracted, and couldn't wait for the hour of prayer to end.
At around forty, something opened, and she spent the rest of her life trying to explain it. Her best-known description is in her life story, written because her confessors asked.
Prayer, she says, is nothing else than close sharing between friends: taking time, often, to be alone with the one we know loves us. Friendship. Not performance, not a list of requests.
Time with a friend who happens to be God.
Later she wrote The Interior Castle, picturing the soul as a castle of one clear crystal, with many rooms, and God living in the very center. Prayer is the door in.
She reformed her order, founding houses where the nuns lived simply, and worked with a young friar who became Saint John of the Cross. She died in 1582.
In 1970, the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone; she and Catherine of Siena were the first women given that title. And she laughed.

teach.h: NO WONDER YOU HAVE SO FEW.
teach.b: People still tell a story, not found in her writings, of her tipping out of a cart into the mud and complaining to God, and hearing, this is how I treat my friends, and answering, then it's no wonder you have so few.
Whether or not it happened, it sounds like someone who talked to God as a friend.

how: Catholics keep Saint Teresa of Ávila's feast on October 15, and her books, especially The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection, are read by Christians of many churches as guides to prayer. Discalced Carmelite nuns still live by her reform.

o: a walled convent where nuns lived apart from the world
a fortress of willpower that keeps temptation out
the soul pictured as a crystal castle, God at its center

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the walled city Teresa came from
the soul as a castle of crystal
the young friar she worked with
the title she was given in 1970

s: prayer came easily to Teresa from the start
for almost twenty years it was a struggle: illness, distraction, waiting for the hour to end.
Teresa was one of the first two women named a Doctor of the Church
'no wonder you have so few friends' is in Teresa's own writings
it's a story people tell about her. it isn't found in her writings.

games.q: you're Teresa. your confessors ask you to explain, in plain words, what prayer is. what do you say?
o: a duty, done at set hours.
a list of requests, carefully made.
games.why: she describes it as close sharing between friends: time alone, often, with the one we know loves us.

practice: If you pray, try Teresa's way: no formal words, just tell God about today as you'd tell a close friend, what annoyed you, what made you laugh, what worries you, then be quiet a moment to let your friend answer.
If not, picture someone who knows you completely and likes you anyway, and tell them.
